Bevan Point

GeometryTrianglesCircles
Game: Move the corners of a triangle and watch a second triangle appear outside it. Its circle always lines up with the first triangle in a surprising way.
How to play: Drag A, B or C with a mouse or finger, or focus a corner and use the arrow keys. Press Check the claims to see what stays true.
Look for the math

Every triangle has three angle bisectors. Extend the outside ones and their crossings form a bigger triangle around the original one. The centre of the big triangle's circle turns out to be exactly opposite the centre of the small triangle's circle.

A triangle hidden in a triangle

The three outside bisectors meet at the excentres Ia, Ib, Ic. They form the excentral triangle. Each side of it is perpendicular to a bisector of the original triangle, so ABC is the orthic triangle of IaIbIc: A, B and C are the feet of its three altitudes.

The altitudes of the big triangle meet at its orthocentre, and that point is the incenter I of ABC. Press Show angle bisectors to see the three lines that make this visible.

One circle does two jobs

A triangle's nine-point circle passes through the feet of its altitudes. The feet of the excentral triangle's altitudes are A, B and C, so its nine-point circle is the circle drawn through ABC. Its centre O is the midpoint of the segment from the big triangle's circumcentre V to its orthocentre I, and its radius is half the big circumradius:

O = (I + V) / 2,   radius(ABC's circle) = radius(Bevan circle) / 2.

The point V is the Bevan point and the big circle is the Bevan circle. Press Show claim 2 to see the line through I, O and V.

The five claims on the article

The archived applet page states them exactly as follows:

  1. I, O, V are collinear and IO = OV.
  2. The circumradius of IaIbIc is twice the circumradius of ABC.
  3. The lines joining V to the excentres are perpendicular to the respective sides of ABC.
  4. I and V are equally far from the Euler line of ABC.
  5. The circumcircle of ABC is the nine-point circle of IaIbIc.

Press Show claim 1 for the right angles in claim 3. The logic test checks all five claims on hundreds of triangles, and compares every point and radius with a second, line-by-line transcription of the applet's own GeoSDoub geometry. All five hold throughout; the only approximation is the average of three distances the applet uses in place of an exact radius.

Try a triangle with a very long, thin shape: the excentres shoot far away, just as they do in the original applet, but O still stays exactly halfway between I and V.

Puzzle by Alexander Bogomolny (cut-the-knot.org)
